record.paper_title: New Open Problems Related to Old Conjectures by Helleseth
record.context_brief: Classify all nice exponents beyond the known families
record.original_question: Let s be an invertible exponent over a finite field of odd characteristic, and write s ≉ 1 to mean that s is not equivalent to 1 under the equivalence generated by s′ ≡ p^j s (mod q − 1) and inversion. Call s nice when the number N(1, v) of solutions to x + y = 1 and x^s + y^s = v takes at most three values as v ranges over the field. The authors found by computation that all nice exponents s ≉ 1 over prime fields of characteristic p < 5000 come from the paradigmatic families in Propositions 6.5 and 6.6. Does every nice exponent s ≉ 1 arise from those paradigmatic examples?

evidence.quote: Definition 6.1. Let s be an invertible exponent over the finite field L. We say that s is a nice exponent over L if the number N(1, v) of solutions in L^2 of x + y = 1, x^s + y^s = v, takes at most 3 values as v runs through L.

Problem 6.7. All nice exponents s ≉ 1 over the prime fields of characteristic p < 5000 were found in the numerical experiment [15], and they all correspond to the paradigmatic examples of Propositions 6.5 and 6.6. Is this a general property?

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Let $p$ be an odd prime and let $L=\mathbb{F}_q$ be a finite field of characteristic $p$ (with $q=p^n$ for some $n\ge 1$). For an integer $s$ coprime to $q-1$ (an invertible exponent over $L$) and for $v\in L$, define
$$N(1,v)=\#\{(x,y)\in L^2:\ x+y=1,\ x^s+y^s=v\}.$$
Call $s$ a nice exponent over $L$ if the multiset $\{N(1,v):v\in L\}$ takes at most three distinct values. On the set of invertible exponents modulo $q-1$, consider the equivalence relation generated by
$$s\sim p^j s\pmod{q-1}\quad\text{and}\quad s\sim s^{-1}\pmod{q-1},$$
and write $s\not\equiv 1$ to mean $s$ is not equivalent to $1$ under this relation.

Two paradigmatic families of nice exponents are known:
(i) exponents $s$ such that $x\mapsto x^s$ is a planar (or near-planar) monomial coming from the classical Dembowski–Ostrom / Coulter–Matthews type constructions over prime fields of odd characteristic, and
(ii) exponents $s$ for which $x^s+x$ is (after a normalization) a power-permutation associated with a Singer-type difference set, yielding a three-valued $N(1,v)$.

(These are the two explicit infinite families that produce nice exponents.)

Question: Is it true that every nice exponent $s\not\equiv 1$ over every prime field $\mathbb{F}_p$ (and more generally over $\mathbb{F}_q$) belongs to one of these two paradigmatic families? Equivalently, classify all nice exponents $s\not\equiv 1$ and prove that no sporadic nice exponents exist beyond the two known families.
artifact.category_tag: finite field exponents and Weil sums
artifact.status_search_result: A web search did not surface any classification result settling whether all nice exponents (in the sense above) reduce to the two known paradigmatic families. Related work on Helleseth's conjectures and Niho-type exponents continues to appear (e.g., Nguyen on Weil sums and Helleseth's conjectures), but none claim a full classification of nice exponents. The problem appears to remain open.

status_evidence.title: On Weil Sums, Conjectures of Helleseth, and Niho Exponents
status_evidence.snippet: Recent work continues to address open conjectures of Helleseth on Weil sums and special exponent classes.
status_evidence.claim: Active research on related Helleseth-type conjectures suggests the classification of nice exponents has not been completed.

status_evidence.title: A survey on the applications of Niho exponents
status_evidence.snippet: Survey of known families of special exponents over finite fields; no full classification of nice exponents is reported.
status_evidence.claim: No source found announcing a classification of all nice exponents beyond known paradigmatic families.
